<p>Statistical methods for large-scale EHR data, where <em>whether</em> a patient is seen and <em>what</em> gets measured are themselves informative about health.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Informative presence</strong> — whether a patient is observed at a given time depends on their underlying condition.</li>
<li><strong>Informative observation</strong> — conditional on a visit, the decision to measure a biomarker is not random.</li>
</ul>
<p>We build joint models that account for these mechanisms so that biomarker trajectories and associations can be estimated without bias.</p>
<div class="pub-ref">
<p>
<strong>C-H. Yang</strong>, X. Shi, B. Mukherjee. (2026). Joint modeling of longitudinal EHR data with shared random effects for informative visiting and observation processes. <em>Biometrics</em> (revised &amp; resubmitted).
</p>
<div class="links">
<a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15374">arXiv ↗</a>
</div>
</div>
<div class="pub-ref">
<p>
J. Du<em>*</em>, <strong>C-H. Yang<em>*</em></strong>, X. Shi, B. Mukherjee. (2026). Analyzing longitudinal outcomes from electronic health records: a joint modeling approach to handle informative visits and observations. <em>Journal of the American Statistical Association</em> (revised &amp; resubmitted). <em>*</em>Co-first authors.
</p>

<li><span class="key key-line key-ctx"></span>pre-tweak</li>

<p>Seamless phase I–II designs for modern oncology that use biological mediators and survival endpoints to optimize dose for targeted therapies and immunotherapies.</p>
<p>This includes the <strong>DEMO</strong> design — a three-stage framework for dose exploration, monitoring, and optimization that selects a dose maximizing restricted mean survival time — and an analysis of the relative conservativeness of the <strong>Bayesian logistic regression method</strong>, with a dose-switching rule that improves performance while maintaining safety.</p>
<div class="pub-ref">
<p>
<strong>C-H. Yang</strong>, P.F. Thall, R. Lin. (2025). Dose exploration, monitoring, and optimization using biological and clinical outcomes. <em>Annals of Applied Statistics</em>, 19(4), 2599–2617.
</p>
<div class="links">
<a href="https://doi.org/10.1214/25-AOAS2099">Paper ↗</a> <a href="https://github.com/ruitaolin/DEMO">Code ↗</a>
</div>
</div>
<div class="pub-ref">
<p>
<strong>C-H. Yang</strong>, G. Cheng, R. Lin. (2024). On the relative conservativeness of the Bayesian logistic regression method in oncology dose-finding studies. <em>Pharmaceutical Statistics</em>, 23(4), 585–594.
</p>
<div class="links">
<a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/pst.2364">Paper ↗</a>

<section id="clinical-trial-methodology" class="level2">
<h2 class="anchored" data-anchor-id="clinical-trial-methodology">Clinical Trial Methodology</h2>
<figure class="area-fig">
<div class="fig-plot"><svg viewBox="0 0 400 180" role="img" aria-labelledby="fig-trials"><title id="fig-trials">Bayesian random-effects dose-optimization meta-analysis</title><line class="axis" x1="120" y1="148" x2="380" y2="148"/><line class="axis" x1="257.8" y1="12" x2="257.8" y2="138"/><line class="ctx" x1="166.8" y1="22" x2="291.6" y2="22"/><rect class="sq" x="225.2" y="18" width="7.9" height="7.9"/><text x="8" y="22" dominant-baseline="central">study 1</text><line class="ctx" x1="218.8" y1="42" x2="307.2" y2="42"/><rect class="sq" x="257.4" y="36.4" width="11.2" height="11.2"/><text x="8" y="42" dominant-baseline="central">study 2</text><line class="ctx" x1="177.2" y1="62" x2="312.4" y2="62"/><rect class="sq" x="241.1" y="58.3" width="7.3" height="7.3"/><text x="8" y="62" dominant-baseline="central">study 3</text><line class="ctx" x1="242.2" y1="82" x2="320.2" y2="82"/><rect class="sq" x="274.9" y="75.7" width="12.7" height="12.7"/><text x="8" y="82" dominant-baseline="central">study 4</text><line class="ctx" x1="205.8" y1="102" x2="299.4" y2="102"/><rect class="sq" x="247.3" y="96.7" width="10.6" height="10.6"/><text x="8" y="102" dominant-baseline="central">study 5</text><polygon class="diamond" points="234.4,128 257.8,121 281.2,128 257.8,135"/><text class="panel" x="8" y="128" dominant-baseline="central">meta-analysis</text><text x="380" y="172" text-anchor="end">efficacy</text></svg></div>
<ul class="fig-key">
<li><span class="key key-sq"></span>small studies</li>
<li><span class="key key-diamond"></span>meta-analysis</li>
</ul>
</figure>
<p>Meta-analytic and model-assisted methods that synthesize evidence and sharpen inference across early-phase trials.</p>
<p><strong>REDOMA</strong> performs random-effects dose-optimization meta-analysis with spike-and-slab priors, allowing plateau or non-monotonic dose-efficacy curves across small studies. <strong>MCP-ModX</strong> adds covariate adjustment to the MCP-Mod framework through g-computation, giving valid and more precise dose-response inference even under model misspecification.</p>
<div class="pub-ref">
<p>
<strong>C-H. Yang</strong>, E. Kwiatkowski, J.J. Lee, R. Lin. (2024). REDOMA: Bayesian random-effects dose-optimization meta-analysis using spike-and-slab priors. <em>Statistics in Medicine</em>, 43(18), 3484–3502.
</p>
<div class="links">
<a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.10107">Paper ↗</a>
</div>
</div>
<div class="pub-ref">
<p>
<strong>C-H. Yang</strong>, R. Lin. (2026). MCP-ModX: multiple comparison procedure and modeling with model-assisted covariate adjustment under missing outcomes. <em>Biometrical Journal</em> (submitted).
</p>
<div class="links">
<a href="https://github.com/cyang728/MCPModX">GitHub ↗</a>
</div>
</div>

<li><span class="key key-line"></span>treatment A</li>
<li><span class="key key-line key-ctx"></span>treatment B</li>
</ul>
</figure>
<p>Model-free methods for individualized treatment decisions in precision medicine.</p>
<p>We developed a <strong>variable screening</strong> method for optimal treatment regimes with high-dimensional survival data that requires no outcome model and no assumed form for the regime, stays valid for any prespecified subgroup, and lets flexible learners such as random forests and boosting be applied to the selected variables.</p>
<div class="pub-ref">
<p>
<strong>C-H. Yang</strong>, Y-J. Cheng. (2024). A model-free variable screening method for optimal treatment regimes with high-dimensional survival data. <em>Biometrika</em>, 111(4), 1369–1386.
</p>
<div class="links">
<a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/asae022">Paper ↗</a>
</div>
</div>
